about: Oldest ceremonies, festivals, folk plays, dances and games, and charitable doles still kept up in the British Isles, each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Ceremony of the Keys, Tower of London
entries.age_text: said to date from the 14th century
entries.claim: said to be the oldest military ceremony still held anywhere in the world
entries.evidence: The Yeoman Warders lock the Tower's main gates every night in a set ritual, said to have been kept up for about 700 years. The 14th-century origin is tradition: Wikipedia says only that it may have begun in the Middle Ages and is often said to go back to the 14th century, and the present words and form are much later.

entries.name: Tynwald Day
entries.age_text: first recorded 24 June 1417; Tynwald traditionally founded 979
entries.claim: the open-air sitting of Tynwald on Tynwald Hill, one of the oldest continuing parliamentary ceremonies; first recorded in 1417
entries.evidence: Each July Tynwald meets in the open air at St John's to promulgate the island's new laws. Its first recorded use for this dates to 24 June 1417; the Viking origin is tradition, and the 979 date celebrated in the 1979 millennium is not documented. The claim to be the world's oldest continuous parliament belongs to Tynwald itself, not only to the ceremony.

sources.quote: Its first recorded use for the promulgation of laws dates to 24 June 1417, when Sir John Stanley presided

entries.name: Dunmow Flitch
entries.claim: a flitch of bacon awarded to married couples who have not quarrelled for a year and a day: known by the late 14th century, first recorded award 1445
entries.evidence: The custom is often dated to 1104 and the Augustinian priory of Little Dunmow, but that story is doubted. Langland and Chaucer allude to the flitch in the late 14th century as something well known, and the earliest surviving record of an award, to Richard Wright, is from the priory's cartulary in 1445. The trials lapsed after 1751 and were revived in the 19th century.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest surviving record of the flitch being awarded, from the cartulary of Dunmow Priory, dates to 1445

entries.name: Puck Fair, Killorglin
entries.age_text: patent of 1613; said to be far older
entries.claim: one of Ireland's oldest fairs, documented from a patent of 1613
entries.evidence: Puck Fair, where a wild goat is crowned king for three days each August, is held to descend from the Lughnasa festival, but it can be traced in documents only to 1613, when a patent allowed a fair on Lammas Day and two days after at Killorglin. Other stories tie the goat to Cromwell's time or to Daniel O'Connell in 1808.

entries.name: Mari Lwyd
entries.claim: the Welsh midwinter custom of the horse's skull, first recorded in 1800
entries.evidence: A horse's skull on a pole, draped in a sheet, is carried from house to house at Christmas and the New Year, its party trading verses for entry. The custom is often called pre-Christian, but the first record of it is from 1800; it was most common in south Wales in the 19th century.

entries.name: The Burryman, South Queensferry
entries.age_text: Ferry Fair granted 1687; custom thought older
entries.claim: a man covered in burrs walks the town on the Ferry Fair's eve; thought older than the fair's grant of 1687, but of unknown origin
entries.evidence: The right to hold the Ferry Fair was first granted in 1687, and the Burryman is widely believed to be older, but nothing earlier is documented; the Ferry Fair's own account traces it back only to living memory of 1746. Its meaning and origin are unclear.

entries.name: Up Helly Aa, Lerwick
entries.age_text: name and torch procession c. 1870; first torch procession on the day 1881
entries.claim: not a Viking survival: a Victorian festival, its name and torch procession devised about 1870 and first held on the day in 1881
entries.evidence: Up Helly Aa grew out of rowdy tar-barrelling at Yule in Lerwick; around 1870 young men gave it its name and a torchlight procession, and the first torch procession on Up Helly Aa Day was in 1881, the galley and Viking costume coming later. Despite claims of ancient origins it is a product of the Victorian era.

entries.category: Oldest folk play, dance or game
entries.name: Abbots Bromley Horn Dance
entries.age_text: hobby-horse dance recorded 1532; one horn radiocarbon-dated 1065 ± 80
entries.claim: one of England's oldest folk dances: recorded from 1532, danced with reindeer horns one of which dates from the 11th century; the 1226 origin is unsupported
entries.evidence: A hobby-horse dance at Abbots Bromley is first recorded in 1532, already called ancient, and the horns are first mentioned in 1686. One reindeer horn was radiocarbon-dated in 1976 to 1065 ± 80, but how and when the horns came to the dance is unknown. The often-repeated start at the St Bartholomew's fair of 1226 has no evidence.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest written record of a hobby-horse performance at Abbots Bromley dates to 1532, and the first mention of the reindeer horns is from 1686

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1976, one of the reindeer horns was radiocarbon dated to 1065 ± 80 years

sources.author: Abbots Bromley Nostalgia
sources.quote: there is no written evidence that a dance originally took place in the 13th century, indeed the earliest reference for a dance (1532) recorded the use of a hobby horse

entries.category: Oldest folk play, dance or game
entries.name: Haxey Hood
entries.claim: said to be one of the oldest surviving traditions in England, by tradition from the 14th century
entries.evidence: On Twelfth Night a mass 'sway' pushes a leather hood to one of the pubs of Haxey or Westwoodside. The legend of Lady de Mowbray's lost hood is dated to about 1359 only by linking it to a land grant of John de Mowbray; no medieval record of the game is known.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This would date the Hood to about 1359 when a deed granting land to commoners was enacted by the baron

sources.title: Haxey Hood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: making it likely to be the oldest surviving tradition in England

sources.title: The Haxey Hood (abstract)

sources.quote: a traditional calendar custom with a history dating back as far as 1359, which takes place on the 6th January

entries.category: Oldest folk play, dance or game
entries.name: Royal Shrovetide Football, Ashbourne
entries.claim: one of the oldest surviving Shrovetide football games, said to be played from at least 1667
entries.evidence: Shrovetide ball games were played in England from at least the 12th century, and the Ashbourne game is said to go back at least to about 1667; its early records were lost in a fire in the 1890s. A University of Derby historian notes that solid evidence of regular play at Ashbourne before the 1810s is hard to find, and that the 1683 poem often cited is not precise about place.

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: although the exact origins of the game are unknown due to a fire at the Royal Shrovetide Committee office in the 1890s which destroyed the earliest records

entries.category: Oldest folk play, dance or game
entries.name: Mummers' play
entries.claim: the mummers' play as known today goes back only to the mid-18th century, not to the Middle Ages or pagan times
entries.evidence: Masked, silent mumming is recorded from the 14th century, but the hero-combat play with St George, a slain champion and a quack doctor cannot be traced before the mid-18th century. The earliest known texts are from the 1770s (a fragment from Exeter may date from 1737); early versions come from Newcastle chapbooks, Dublin, Exeter and Revesby in Lincolnshire.

sources.title: Mummers' play (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest evidence of mummers' plays as they are known today is from the mid- to late 18th century

sources.title: English Folk Drama – Earliest References
sources.author: English Folk Dance and Song Society
sources.quote: The unromantic fact is that the mumming play cannot be traced back any earlier than the mid-eighteenth century

sources.title: The mummers' play
sources.author: Traditional Drama Research Group (folkplay.info)
sources.quote: Our earliest examples come from the eighteenth century and include printed versions in chapbooks from Newcastle-upon-Tyne

entries.name: Wayfarer's Dole, Hospital of St Cross
entries.age_text: hospital founded 1132–36; dole of unknown date
entries.claim: bread and ale given to any traveller who asks, at what is said to be England's oldest charitable institution
entries.evidence: Henry of Blois founded the Hospital of St Cross at Winchester between 1132 and 1136, and it still gives the Wayfarer's Dole, a horn cup of ale and a piece of bread, to anyone who asks at the Porter's Lodge. The dole is said to have been started by a Cluniac monk, but when it began is not documented, so its age is that of tradition.

sources.title: Hospital of St Cross (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Hospital continues an ancient tradition in the "Wayfarer's Dole", which consists of a small horn cup of ale and a piece of bread

entries.name: Tichborne Dole
entries.claim: a yearly gift of flour on Lady Day, said to date from the 12th century
entries.evidence: Each 25 March flour blessed by a priest is given out at Tichborne House to the people of Tichborne and Cheriton. The founding by Lady Mabella Tichborne, who crawled round the field still called the Crawls, is a legend dated to about 1150; it was painted in 1671 and paused in the 1790s, but no medieval record of it is cited.

sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The festival dates back to the 12th century (c. 1150) and was started by Lady Mabella Tichborne

sources.title: The Tichborne Dole

sources.quote: Lady Mabella succeeded in crawling around a twenty-three acre field which is still called ‘The Crawls’ to this day

entries.name: Royal Maundy
entries.claim: the monarch's Maundy Thursday gifts to the poor, first recorded under King John in 1210
entries.evidence: King John is the first English monarch recorded giving Maundy alms, at Knaresborough on 15 April 1210, and in 1213 he gave silver pennies to thirteen poor men. The monarch still gives specially minted Maundy money each year, now to pensioners chosen for service to their communities, as many men and women as the sovereign's years.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first English monarch to be recorded as distributing alms at a Maundy service was John, who on 15 April 1210 donated garments

sources.title: Royal Maundy Service
sources.author: The Royal Household
sources.quote: Every Maundy Thursday, the Monarch distributes special Maundy money to local pensioners in a service which commemorates Jesus washing the feet of the Apostles at the Last Supper
